articles.topic: Loneliness steals years of healthy life
articles.headline: Your Isolation Might Cost You 6 Years. The New Science Is Personal.
articles.body: A major study tracking over 277,000 adults just found something worth paying attention to. Loneliness and social isolation aren't just uncomfortable—they're expensive in terms of actual years lived well. Men who were both lonely and isolated lost about 5.8 years free from depression and anxiety. Women lost roughly 3.7 years. The hit to mental health was sharper than to physical health, but both matter. The distinction matters too: loneliness (feeling alone) and isolation (actually lacking community) are different problems requiring different fixes.
articles.takeaway: Check your calendar. If you haven't seen friends or family in weeks, that's not a lifestyle choice—it's a longevity risk. Prioritize it like you would exercise.

articles.headline: The One Thing Parkinson's Patients Are Getting Right
articles.body: New research from the University of Cincinnati just published something that matters for anyone getting older. People with Parkinson's who moved more—over eight hours weekly of physical activity—saw slower decline in both thinking and movement. The benefits stacked. More hours meant more protection. What kind of movement? Brisk walking, swimming, cycling, household work. Nothing exotic. The researchers followed participants for up to seven years and found that even modest increases in regular activity created measurable protection for memory and motor control.
articles.takeaway: You don't need a gym membership or a program. Consistent movement, eight-plus hours per week split across gentle and vigorous activity, appears to protect your brain and body from decline.

articles.topic: Optimism buffers chronic stress and heart health
articles.headline: Your Mindset Actually Changes Your Heart Risk
articles.body: Young adults facing high chronic stress showed worse cardiovascular health markers. That's the bad news. The good news: researchers at the University of Massachusetts found that optimism and social support acted as buffers. They mediated 26% and 10% of the stress-heart connection respectively. This wasn't about ignoring stress. It was about how stress traveled through your body. Optimism didn't stop stress from happening—it changed what stress did to your cardiovascular system. Social support did the same thing. Both created a pathway that short-circuited the physical damage.
articles.takeaway: If you're under real pressure, don't waste energy trying to avoid it. Build your optimism network. Choose your people. That actually rewires how your body responds.

articles.topic: Dance outperforms all exercise for cognition
articles.headline: The Brain Exercise That Works Better Than You Think
articles.body: Researchers reviewed 209 randomized trials comparing dance to every other exercise style—aerobic work, strength training, tai chi, stretching. Dance won. It topped the list for overall cognition. It ranked in the top tier for working memory, attention, physical performance, and mood. Why? Probably because dance stacks multiple demands simultaneously: rhythm, balance, coordination, memory, social connection. You're not just moving. You're thinking while moving. You're responding in real time. Your brain has to fire on all cylinders. It's also inherently social and genuinely enjoyable, which means people actually stick with it.
articles.takeaway: If you hate treadmills, stop using them as your cognitive defense. Find music. Find rhythm. Find other people. Dance delivers what gym time doesn't.

workout.title: Steady State Foundation: 40-Minute Conversational Base Run
workout.tip: If you can't say a full sentence, you're too fast. Zone 2 feels *easy*—embrace the lack of urgency. This builds the aerobic engine that makes race paces feel sustainable.
workout.warmup: 5 min easy jog + 3 × 20 sec dynamic leg swings (forward/back, side-to-side), 10 walking lunges

exercises.name: Continuous Zone 2 Run
exercises.notes: Maintain conversational pace (120–140 bpm estimated). Focus on nasal breathing when possible; if mouth breathing becomes necessary, you're above Z2. Cadence should feel relaxed, around 170–180 steps per minute. This is aerobic base work—no speed goals, only consistency.

workout.cooldown: 3 min easy walking + standing quad stretch 30 sec each leg, forward fold 45 sec, calf stretch 30 sec each leg
workout.description: A pure Zone 2 aerobic run at conversational pace—the cornerstone of endurance fitness for 5K, 10K, half-marathon, and marathon athletes. This "boring" work builds aerobic capacity, improves fat oxidation, and accelerates recovery between harder sessions. Intermediate runners will target 120–140 bpm (or a pace where you can speak in full sentences) for the entire 40 minutes.

meal.title: Seared Chicken Thighs with Warm Lentil and Roasted Pepper Salad
meal.description: Cook a double batch of lentils on Sunday and this meal comes together in under 15 minutes on a weeknight.
ingredients: 1 cup cooked green or puy lentils
1 roasted red pepper (jarred is fine), sliced
Salt and black pepper to taste
meal.instructions: Season chicken thighs with smoked paprika, salt, and pepper. Sear skin-side down in an oven-safe pan over medium-high heat for 6-7 minutes until golden, then flip and finish in a 400F oven for 12-15 minutes until cooked through. While chicken rests, warm olive oil in a pan over medium heat and saute garlic for 1 minute. Add lentils, roasted pepper, and spinach. Stir until spinach wilts, then deglaze with red wine vinegar. Serve the lentil salad topped with the chicken thigh and a scatter of fresh parsley.
